paragraphs: This paper asks whether reducing the cost of a neural network must weaken its ability to represent smooth functions. It studies low-rank compression, where a large weight matrix is replaced by a product of smaller matrices. The proposed network implements this structure by placing narrow, bias-free linear layers between adjacent nonlinear layers.

The central result concerns fixed-depth networks using the Swish activation. The authors prove that these networks can approximate any function in a specified Hölder ball on a unit cube to arbitrarily small error. This function class is defined by smoothness and radius parameters, so the guarantee concerns a mathematically specified family of smooth functions.

Their construction needs linear hidden layers no wider than one-third of the nonlinear layers. This implies at least a one-third reduction in computational cost relative to a network with the same depth and nonlinear-layer widths but without those narrow layers. The contribution is a constructive approximation guarantee: substantial low-rank structure can coexist with strong representational capability.
icml-2025-approximation-to-smooth-functi.tldr: Fixed-depth, low-rank Swish networks can approximate a specified class of smooth functions arbitrarily well while reducing computational cost.

paragraphs: Analyzing tables through conversation requires an assistant to handle an evolving exchange rather than answer a single isolated question. Evaluating that ability is difficult because realistic conversational records are costly to collect. This paper introduces CoTA, a benchmark containing 1,013 conversations across four named settings: Normal, Action, Private, and Private Action.

The authors construct the benchmark using Decision Company, a multi-agent environment intended to produce conversational data with limited human effort. A study involving data analysis experts finds that the environment generates diverse, high-quality data. This makes the data-generation process part of the contribution, alongside the benchmark used to assess language models.

Evaluations expose challenges for current models in conversational table analysis. The authors also introduce Adaptive Conversation Reflection, which generates reflections from successful conversation histories to guide subsequent behavior. Experiments report relative performance improvements of up to 35.14%. The findings suggest that learning from successful interactions can improve conversational analysis, while CoTA provides a way to measure those improvements.
icml-2025-are-large-language-models-read.tldr: CoTA benchmarks conversational table analysis, and a reflection strategy improves evaluated language models by up to 35.14% relatively.

paragraphs: Generative models can make consequential decisions within a surprisingly short part of generation. Language models may abruptly change behavior, while diffusion models can settle important output features during narrow critical windows. This paper develops a shared theoretical explanation for these phenomena across both autoregressive generation and diffusion.

The explanation uses stochastic localization: as generation proceeds, the process narrows toward a subpopulation of the distribution being modeled. The authors show that critical windows emerge generically through this narrowing. Their analysis requires few distributional assumptions and basic mathematical tools, extending beyond earlier diffusion theories tied closely to Gaussian diffusion and stronger assumptions about the data.

The theory also improves previous quantitative bounds when applied specifically to diffusion models. Empirical tests with language models support its predictions, and critical windows often coincide with failures on mathematical and reasoning problems. That observation connects a general property of generation to practical reasoning behavior, while establishing coincidence rather than claiming that every critical window causes a failure.
icml-2025-blink-of-an-eye-a-simple-theor.tldr: A unified theory explains narrow decision windows in generative models as generation narrows toward a subpopulation of possible outputs.

paragraphs: Generating a plausible time series is only part of the challenge when an application needs particular domain characteristics or temporal patterns. This paper introduces text-controlled time-series generation, where written descriptions guide the generated sequence. Text provides a way to express semantic information, domain context, and requirements for an individual example.

The approach tackles both data availability and generation. An LLM-based multi-agent framework synthesizes paired descriptions and time series to address scarce training data. The Bridge generation framework then combines textual descriptions with semantic prototypes to provide domain-level guidance. Together, these components connect the desired behavior described in language with the production of tailored temporal data.

Bridge achieves state-of-the-art generation fidelity on 11 of the 12 evaluated datasets. Compared with generation without text input, it improves controllability by up to 12% on mean squared error and 6% on mean absolute error. These findings support text as a useful control channel in the evaluated settings, with gains in both realism and adherence to requested characteristics.
icml-2025-bridge-bootstrapping-text-to-c.tldr: Bridge combines synthetic text–time-series training data with textual and prototype guidance to improve time-series realism and controllability.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can produce high-quality speech, but repeatedly removing noise makes generation expensive. Compressing this process through distillation has also tended to reduce quality. DMOSpeech addresses both issues with a distilled text-to-speech model that, in the reported experiments, generates speech faster and performs better than its teacher model.

Its key design enables gradients to reach every model component, allowing differentiable evaluation objectives to directly guide end-to-end training. The method incorporates Connectionist Temporal Classification loss and Speaker Verification loss. This addresses a barrier in previous systems, where non-differentiable components or iterative sampling prevented direct optimization of the complete synthesis process using these metrics.

The authors report improvements in naturalness, intelligibility, and similarity to the target speaker, supported by extensive human evaluation. They also report inference-time reductions of orders of magnitude. The findings connect the computational benefit of distillation with a training benefit: a more directly optimizable synthesis model can improve perceptual results while substantially shortening the generation process.
icml-2025-dmospeech-direct-metric-optimi.tldr: DMOSpeech uses distilled diffusion and direct metric optimization to generate speech faster while outperforming its teacher in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: A useful code edit must introduce the requested change while preserving the program’s intended functionality. This paper argues that treating editing as an implicit input-to-output task overlooks the explicit steps involved in transforming code. EditLord makes those steps visible by learning reusable transformation rules from examples of code before and after editing.

A language model acts as an inductive learner, extracting concise sets of meta-rules from training pairs. Those rules are then expressed for individual training examples. The resulting guidance can augment fine-tuning data or support editing through prompts and iterative procedures, allowing the same framework to operate across several ways of using a language model.

Across the evaluated software engineering and security applications, models, and editing modes, EditLord reports average gains of 22.7% in editing performance and 58.1% in robustness over the state of the art, alongside 20.2% higher functional correctness. These results support explicit transformation knowledge as a useful mechanism for improving both requested changes and preservation of program behavior.
icml-2025-editlord-learning-code-transfo.tldr: EditLord learns explicit code-transformation rules from examples to improve editing performance, robustness, and functional correctness.

paragraphs: Removing rain streaks requires restoring background content while identifying the visual structure associated with rain. Fourier-based methods use frequency information for this purpose, but the paper argues that they underuse relationships between low and high frequencies. FourierMamba introduces Mamba into Fourier space to model these relationships during image restoration.

The framework treats spatial and channel frequency information differently because their frequency orders are arranged differently. In the spatial case, it uses a zigzag scan to reorder frequencies from low to high before modeling their connections. In the channel case, frequencies already have an ordered arrangement along the axis, allowing Mamba to model their relationships directly.

This design makes frequency ordering a central part of how the model learns, rather than using the same scan for both dimensions. Experiments report better qualitative and quantitative results than state-of-the-art deraining methods. The stated findings support combining Fourier information with correlation modeling that respects the distinct organization of spatial and channel frequencies.
icml-2025-fouriermamba-fourier-learning-.tldr: FourierMamba improves image deraining by using distinct spatial and channel scans to model relationships between Fourier frequencies.

paragraphs: Naive Bayes remains useful because of its simplicity, effectiveness, and robustness, but this paper identifies an opportunity to improve its handling of numerical attributes. The proposed method, instance correlation graph-based naive Bayes, incorporates relationships among data examples into the information available to a Gaussian naive Bayes classifier.

The method first builds a graph from the original attributes, using it to represent correlations among instances. A variational graph auto-encoder then produces new attributes from that graph. These learned attributes supplement the original ones, giving the final classifier access to information derived from how examples relate to one another.

Before fitting Gaussian naive Bayes, the method weights the augmented attributes to reduce redundancy. This matters because adding graph-derived information can also introduce overlapping signals. Experiments across tens of datasets report significant improvements over the evaluated competitors. The contribution is therefore a staged integration of instance relationships, learned features, and attribute weighting within a naive Bayes classification pipeline.
icml-2025-instance-correlation-graph-bas.tldr: ICGNB augments Gaussian naive Bayes with graph-derived attributes that capture correlations among examples, then weights attributes to reduce redundancy.

paragraphs: A robustness benchmark becomes harder to interpret when its supposedly unfamiliar distortions already occur in training data. The paper argues that this affects older image benchmarks: web-scale datasets contain common effects such as blur and compression artifacts. Strong benchmark scores may therefore reflect exposure to those distortions as well as an ability to generalize.

LAION-C introduces six new distortion types designed to remain out of distribution even for web-scale datasets such as LAION. The authors evaluate contemporary vision models, including multimodal language models such as Gemini and GPT-4o, and find that these distortions present substantial challenges. The benchmark aims to provide a more informative test under this changed training regime.

The study also includes a psychophysical experiment measuring human performance on the corruptions under laboratory conditions. In these comparisons, the best models match or outperform the best human observers. That result concerns the evaluated distortions and tasks; it shows that challenging new robustness tests can coexist with model performance reaching or exceeding the measured human level.
icml-2025-laion-c-an-out-of-distribution.tldr: LAION-C tests web-scale vision models with six new distortions and finds substantial challenges alongside top models matching or exceeding measured human performance.

paragraphs: Deep clustering learns to group examples without access to labels, so its training must obtain supervision from other signals. Common choices include similarities between examples and labels estimated by the model itself. This paper examines another source: how consistently each individual example is represented as training progresses across epochs.

The authors connect this sample-level stability with clustering accuracy and the network’s ability to memorize individual examples. Representations that change substantially across epochs often correspond to incorrect predictions, difficulty in memorization, and atypical examples. This is a relationship observed during training, making the behavior of each sample over time informative for constructing supervision.

Building on these findings, the paper introduces training signals based on stability at the representation level. The strategy is designed to enhance multiple deep clustering techniques, and benchmark experiments show that incorporating it can improve performance. The practical contribution is a way to use the training trajectory itself to guide unsupervised learning, supplementing signals based on similarities or estimated labels.
icml-2025-learning-from-sample-stability.tldr: Tracking how stable each example’s representation remains across training provides supervision that can improve deep clustering.

paragraphs: Long visual and textual inputs make a vision-language model’s initial processing expensive because attention has quadratic complexity. MMInference targets this pre-filling stage with dynamic sparse attention. Its design starts from an analysis showing that video’s spatial and temporal locality creates a distinctive grid pattern, while different modalities have different sparse attention distributions.

The method uses a permutation-based approach to exploit the grid structure and address boundaries between modalities. An offline search selects sparse patterns for each attention head, and the attention distribution is then constructed dynamically for the actual input. Optimized GPU kernels turn these structured sparse computations into an efficient implementation.

MMInference integrates into existing vision-language pipelines without modifying the model or fine-tuning it. Tests across video question answering, captioning, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks report pre-filling speedups of up to 8.3 times at one million tokens while maintaining accuracy. The result specifically concerns faster processing of the supplied context, showing the value of adapting sparse attention to multimodal structure.
icml-2025-mminference-accelerating-pre-f.tldr: MMInference exploits modality-specific sparse attention patterns to accelerate million-token pre-filling by up to 8.3 times while maintaining evaluated accuracy.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models benefit from scaling through multiple experts, but their parameter counts create substantial memory demands. MoE-SVD compresses these models without additional training. It uses singular value decomposition to express expert weights through compact, low-rank matrices, with the aim of reducing memory use and accelerating inference.

The framework selectively decomposes expert layers according to sensitivity measurements derived from weight singular values and activation statistics. It then shares a single V matrix across experts and uses a top-k selection for U matrices. This combination of selective decomposition, sharing, and trimming addresses matrix redundancy while seeking to preserve differences among experts.

Experiments cover Mixtral, Phi-3.5, DeepSeek, and Qwen2 mixture-of-experts models. The authors report better results than other compression methods, with a 60% compression ratio and 1.5 times faster inference alongside minimal performance loss. These findings support compression tailored to expert structure, where deciding what to decompose and share is central to retaining useful model behavior.
icml-2025-moe-svd-structured-mixture-of-.tldr: MoE-SVD selectively decomposes and shares expert matrices to compress mixture-of-experts models without extra training and with minimal reported performance loss.

paragraphs: Adversarially trained networks can perform well on unseen natural inputs while failing to extend their training-set robustness to unseen inputs. This paper calls that combination clean generalization and robust overfitting. It studies the phenomenon through two complementary questions: what a network can represent, and what its training dynamics lead it to learn.

For binary classification with N separated training points in D dimensions, the authors assume a clean classifier of size polynomial in D exists. Under that assumption, a ReLU network can exhibit the phenomenon through robust memorization using only O(ND) extra parameters. By comparison, representing a robust classifier can require exponential complexity in the worst case.

The training analysis considers structured data and a two-layer convolutional network of O(ND) width trained against adversarial perturbations. It proves a three-stage learning transition that ends in robust memorization, producing the same generalization mismatch. Experiments on real-image recognition datasets support the analysis. The results explain how fitting adversarial training examples can remain compatible with good clean performance yet inadequate robust generalization.
icml-2025-on-the-clean-generalization-an.tldr: Under specified theoretical settings, robust memorization explains how adversarial training can yield good clean generalization but poor robust generalization.

paragraphs: Next-token prediction is central to pretraining decoder-only language models, but its empirical success leaves theoretical questions about generalization. This paper develops a fine-grained analysis of how models trained with that objective can generalize. A central concern is that tokens within a sequence are dependent, which the analysis explicitly addresses.

The authors use Rademacher complexity and develop a decomposition that separates the model’s representation learner from its token predictor. They also establish covering-number upper bounds for transformers with multiple layers and attention heads under the Frobenius norm. Their treatment incorporates the mask matrix used within self-attention, connecting the bounds to the decoder’s attention structure.

The resulting theory quantifies dependence on the number of training sequences, the maximum sequence length, and the model’s parameter count. Experiments on public datasets support the theoretical findings. The contribution is a more detailed account of how data size, sequence structure, and model scale enter generalization analysis for next-token pretraining, including the dependence between tokens.
icml-2025-on-the-generalization-ability-.tldr: A generalization analysis of next-token pretraining accounts for token dependence and quantifies the roles of sequence count, sequence length, and model size.

paragraphs: Federated learning must combine learning across participants whose data distributions can differ substantially. Sharpness-aware minimization has been used to improve local learning under this heterogeneity. The paper identifies two shortcomings in many such methods: they do not directly account for the global objective, and each iteration requires two backward passes.

FedGMT uses the trajectory of the global model to measure sharpness for the global objective directly. This connects the local training procedure to information about how the shared model evolves. The proposed method requires only one backward pass, addressing the computational cost at the same time as the mismatch between local and global optimization.

The authors provide a convergence analysis and evaluate FedGMT on visual and text datasets across several scenarios. They report accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art federated methods while minimizing computation and communication overhead. The findings support the global model trajectory as a useful source of optimization information when heterogeneous local data complicates learning a shared model.
icml-2025-one-arrow-two-hawks-sharpness-.tldr: FedGMT uses the global model trajectory for sharpness-aware federated learning with one backward pass and competitive reported accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper argues that language models’ proof abilities depend heavily on whether relevant proof procedures appeared during training. To probe conceptual reasoning, it focuses on counterexamples: examples that expose why a mathematical assertion does not hold. This draws on a teaching approach that uses concrete cases to clarify the scope of mathematical concepts.

The authors manually construct COUNTERMATH, a university-level benchmark requiring counterexample-based mathematical reasoning. Its purpose is to assess whether models can use mathematical concepts to produce the required examples. They also develop a data engineering framework that automatically obtains training data, connecting the evaluation task with a route toward improving model capabilities.

Experiments and analyses find the benchmark challenging, including for OpenAI o1, and identify insufficient counterexample-driven proof capability in evaluated models. Training explorations indicate that strengthening this form of conceptual reasoning is important for broader mathematical improvement. The work therefore contributes both an assessment of a specific reasoning weakness and a method for supplying training data aimed at that weakness.
icml-2025-one-example-shown-many-concept.tldr: COUNTERMATH tests mathematical reasoning through counterexamples and supports training approaches aimed at improving this challenging capability.

paragraphs: This paper studies classification when one class dominates the data and several others are rare. Jointly fitting a multiclass logistic regression model can be computationally challenging in this setting. Motivated by TikTok live-stream data, the authors investigate whether simpler estimation problems can retain the statistical benefits of the full model.

Their theoretical analysis indicates that the maximum likelihood estimators for different rare classes are asymptotically independent. This motivates fitting separate two-class logistic regression problems, each pairing a rare class with the major class. The resulting problems are easier to compute and can run fully in parallel. A further variant downsamples the major class to reduce computation.

Under appropriate regularity conditions, the authors prove that the proposed estimators can match the asymptotic efficiency of the global maximum likelihood estimator. The guarantee concerns limiting statistical behavior under those conditions, rather than identical estimates in every dataset. Simulations support the theoretical findings, and analysis of TikTok live-stream data illustrates the approach in its motivating application.
icml-2025-pairwise-maximum-likelihood-fo.tldr: Separate rare-versus-majority logistic regressions can match joint estimation’s asymptotic efficiency under suitable conditions while enabling cheaper, parallel computation.

paragraphs: Prediction-powered inference improves statistical estimation by combining limited gold-standard observations with machine-learning predictions. This paper extends that idea to applications asking many statistical questions simultaneously. Its method, Prediction-Powered Adaptive Shrinkage, estimates multiple means by combining prediction-powered inference with empirical Bayes shrinkage, allowing related estimation tasks to inform one another.

The method gives predictions two roles. Within each task, it corrects bias in noisy machine-learning predictions. Across tasks, it uses those same predictions as reference points for shrinkage. The amount of shrinkage is selected by minimizing an unbiased estimate of risk, giving the method a data-driven way to determine how strongly to use these reference points.

The authors prove that this tuning strategy is asymptotically optimal. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that the method adapts to prediction reliability and outperforms traditional and modern baselines in large-scale applications. The contribution is a unified approach to correcting prediction errors within individual tasks while borrowing statistical strength across a collection of tasks.
icml-2025-prediction-powered-adaptive-sh.tldr: Prediction-Powered Adaptive Shrinkage combines within-task prediction debiasing with cross-task shrinkage and an asymptotically optimal tuning strategy.

paragraphs: Guidance is widely used to improve samples from diffusion models, yet theoretical explanations have often covered only narrowly specified data distributions. This paper moves beyond analyses restricted to isotropic Gaussian classes or one-dimensional supports with extra conditions. It studies how guidance affects sample quality under more general data distributions.

A central distinction is between improving every sample and improving the population of generated samples. The authors explicitly observe that uniform quality improvement does not hold for some distributions. They therefore analyze the fraction of bad samples, with badness measured through classifier probability, instead of requiring each individual generated result to become better.

The paper proves that guidance can reduce this bad-sample ratio. This gives a theoretical meaning to overall quality improvement that is compatible with individual exceptions. The result matters because it supports the motivation for guidance beyond earlier special cases while keeping the guarantee tied to a specific aggregate measure of quality: the proportion of samples judged bad by classifier probability.
icml-2025-provable-efficiency-of-guidanc.tldr: For general data distributions, diffusion guidance can reduce the proportion of bad samples without improving every sample individually.

paragraphs: Multimodal models can have strong language reasoning yet weaker visual perception. Using multiple vision experts helps provide diverse representations at different levels of detail, but the model still needs to combine them effectively. This paper finds that a router trained end to end does not always choose the best expert weights for each test example.

R2-T2 adjusts those routing weights during testing. It locally moves the current example’s weight vector toward routing vectors associated with correctly predicted examples in its neighborhood. The method therefore changes how existing expert representations are mixed for the current input. The authors propose three strategies that differ in their optimization objectives and where they search for neighbors.

Across challenging multimodal benchmarks covering diverse tasks, R2-T2 consistently and significantly improves the evaluated state-of-the-art models. It does so without training parameters in the base model. The findings identify test-time expert mixing as a useful target for improvement: the available representations can become more effective when the router’s choice is refined for individual inputs.
icml-2025-r2-t2-re-routing-in-test-time-.tldr: R2-T2 improves multimodal models by refining expert-routing weights at test time using nearby correctly predicted examples.

paragraphs: Model editing updates a language model’s stored knowledge by changing parameters without retraining the model. Repeated editing creates an additional challenge: every update changes the parameter state that future edits must work with. Hypernetworks that generate edits can struggle when their update rules do not accommodate this continuing evolution.

RLEdit treats hypernetwork-based lifelong editing as a reinforcement-learning problem. It uses editing losses as rewards and optimizes the hypernetwork over an entire sequence of knowledge updates. This sequence-level objective is intended to help the editor track changes in the language model and produce parameter updates appropriate to its evolving state.

Evaluations across several language models report better lifelong editing effectiveness and efficiency than existing methods. The abstract reports a 59.24% improvement and time consumption equal to only 2.11% of that required by most compared approaches. The central finding is that accounting for a sequence of edits during optimization can improve an editor’s ability to keep updating a model as its parameters change.
icml-2025-reinforced-lifelong-editing-fo.tldr: RLEdit trains a hypernetwork with reinforcement learning over edit sequences to improve repeated knowledge updates as a language model changes.

paragraphs: This paper examines why safety alignment can remain vulnerable to adversarial requests. The authors identify a problem with expecting a model to learn safety-related reasoning implicitly during alignment: competing objectives can dilute the safety signal. As a result, the model may struggle to maintain a clear safety decision boundary under attack.

The proposed approach introduces an explicit binary safety-classification task and integrates its signals into attention and decoding. Safety assessment can then consider both the incoming query and tokens already generated at each necessary generation step. This makes the safety judgment an explicit part of the response-generation process rather than leaving it entirely implicit in alignment training.

The authors report an overhead cost below 0.2 times the original cost and significant improvements in resilience against various adversarial attacks. These findings support explicit safety signals as a practical way to strengthen the evaluated models’ responses to malicious queries. The reported improvement concerns resistance across tested attacks, while the mechanism addresses how safety information influences ongoing generation.
icml-2025-safety-alignment-can-be-not-su.tldr: Explicit safety classification integrated with attention and decoding improves reported attack resilience with less than 0.2 times additional overhead.

paragraphs: Preference learning trains language models using comparisons between candidate responses. This paper investigates the choice between on-policy and off-policy preference data, motivated by conflicting findings about which works better. Its experiments find complementary strengths: on-policy data helps particularly with mathematical and coding reasoning, while off-policy data performs better on subjective tasks such as creative writing and recommendations.

SimpleMix uses these findings to motivate directly mixing the two data sources. The approach aims to combine their benefits across tasks without introducing a complicated method for coordinating them. The key contribution is the empirical case that the choice of data source should reflect complementary task strengths rather than a single preferred source.

Across diverse tasks and benchmarks, SimpleMix improves alignment. On Alpaca Eval 2.0, it reports an average gain of 6.03 over on-policy and off-policy DPO, and an average gain of 3.05 over the more complex HyPO and DPO-Mix-P approaches. These results support simple data mixing as an effective and efficient preference-learning strategy in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-simplemix-frustratingly-simple.tldr: SimpleMix combines on-policy and off-policy preference data to exploit their complementary strengths across reasoning and subjective tasks.

paragraphs: Satisfiability Modulo Counting combines logical constraints with probabilistic inference: some Boolean truth values depend on probabilistic calculations. Approximate solvers can produce answers that violate constraints. Combining separate exact logical and probabilistic solvers avoids that problem, but repeated calls back and forth between them can make solving slow.

KOCO-SMC integrates the processes in an exact solver using probabilistic circuits. It tracks lower and upper bounds during probabilistic inference, enabling useful estimation before every variable has been assigned. This allows the solver to work with partial assignments, whereas the existing methods described in the paper require complete assignments for their probabilistic evaluations.

The authors compare KOCO-SMC with available approximate and exact solvers on large-scale datasets and real-world applications. They report that it finds exact solutions in much less time. The contribution is a way to preserve exactness while making probabilistic information available earlier in the logical search, reducing the cost associated with repeatedly coordinating separate solving processes.
icml-2025-solving-satisfiability-modulo-.tldr: KOCO-SMC speeds up exact reasoning with logical and probabilistic constraints by tracking inference bounds under partial variable assignments.

paragraphs: An image containing several objects can imply several possible sound sources, making it difficult to generate audio for the object a user intends. This paper develops an interactive model that grounds sound generation in selected image objects. The user’s visual selection becomes the basis for deciding which object the generated audio should correspond to.

The model combines object-centric learning with conditional latent diffusion. Multimodal attention learns associations between image regions and their corresponding sounds. At test time, image segmentation supports object-level interaction, allowing the system to use the selected region when generating audio. This connects learning visual–audio relationships with a concrete mechanism for user control.

The authors provide theoretical validation that their attention mechanism functionally approximates the segmentation masks used at test time. This supports the connection between learned attention and object selection. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations show better alignment between objects and generated sounds than the compared baselines. The stated result is more accurate object-grounded audio generation within scenes containing multiple potential sources.
icml-2025-sounding-that-object-interacti.tldr: An object-aware diffusion model generates audio for user-selected image regions and improves alignment between selected objects and their sounds.
